title: Container Ship Inspection: Hatch Corners, Cell Guides and Decks
description: How container ships are inspected: hatch corner fatigue, thick deck plating, cell guides, lashing bridges, pontoon covers and the UR Z7 hull survey cycle.
h1: How Container Ships Are Inspected: Upper Deck, Hatch Covers, Holds and Surveys
intro: A container ship is an open box. Its huge hatch openings leave little deck plating, so the hull's bending and twisting strength is carried by the coaming tops, the sheer strake and the side tanks beneath them. That design decides where surveyors look and where defects appear. This guide explains how container ships are surveyed under the general IACS hull rules, where fatigue cracks, contact damage and corrosion usually turn up, what the large-ship rules on thick plating mean in service, and what owners check before a docking, a redelivery or a sale.

highlights.h: Cracks start where the deck is narrowest
highlights.p: Hatch corners, coaming top ends, cross-deck strips and the sheer strake carry the highest stresses in an open hull. Fatigue cracks in these details are found at close range after cleaning, and confirmed with magnetic particle testing before anyone decides on a repair.

Dedicated container ships sit outside the enhanced survey programme and outside the general dry cargo requirements of UR Z7.1. They are surveyed under UR Z7, with IACS Recommendation 84 as the reference for typical damage and repairs, so the owner shapes much of the gauging plan.

Containers lowered against cell guides, spreaders striking coamings and heavy stacks on pontoon covers all leave damage behind. Owners record it at delivery, at redelivery and before a sale, because damage discovered months after a charter has ended is hard to attribute to anyone.

sections.h: Why are container ships inspected differently from other cargo ships?
p: On a bulk carrier or a tanker the main deck is a continuous plate working as the top flange of the hull girder. On a container ship most of that deck has been cut away for the hatches, leaving narrow strips outboard of the coamings and between the openings. Longitudinal strength moves into the hatch side coamings, the coaming top plates, the deck strips and the sheer strake, and twisting stiffness is recovered by the torsion box along each side, formed by the upper deck, side shell, inner side and a stringer deck below.

Three consequences follow. Stress concentrates wherever this upper structure changes shape: at hatch corners, at coaming ends and where the open hull meets the deckhouse and forecastle. The ship flexes and twists more than a closed-deck ship, so fatigue rather than corrosion tends to produce the earliest serious defects. And the fittings that guide and secure containers take daily contact damage that a surveyor sees at every visit.

sections.h: Which IACS survey rules apply to a container ship?
p: UR Z7, Hull Classification Surveys, applies to all self-propelled ships, and for a dedicated container ship it is the governing hull survey requirement. The ship is not one of the ESP types covered by SOLAS chapter XI-1, and UR Z7.1, which deals with general dry cargo ships, lists dedicated container carriers among the ships it excludes. Annual surveys fall within three months either side of each anniversary date, an intermediate survey replaces the second or third annual, and UR Z3 calls for at least two examinations of the outside of the bottom in each five-year period, with no more than 36 months between any two.

The minimum thickness measurement extent rises with each special survey, as the table shows. For ships under 100 m long, which covers many feeders, UR Z7 allows fewer transverse sections at the third and later surveys. These are floors, not targets: the surveyor extends readings wherever findings justify it.

sections.h: Hatch corners, coaming tops and the sheer strake: where do fatigue cracks start?
p: The hatch corner is the classic container ship detail. The deck plating is cut to a radius or an elliptical curve to spread stress where the opening meets the deck strip, and any notch in that edge can start a crack that grows with every voyage: a rough flame cut, a spatter mark, a temporary fitting cut away, or a corrosion pit. The same applies where coaming top plates and their brackets terminate, and at deckhouse and engine casing corners.

The sheer strake works with the deck as part of the upper flange. Where it is welded to the deck stringer rather than rounded into it, the gunwale weld is a fatigue detail of its own, and the shell longitudinals inside the torsion box carry cyclic loads from hull bending and sea pressure alike. Bulwark ends, chocks and fairleads welded to the sheer strake add stress raisers.

Paint cracking along a weld toe or corner edge is the usual early sign. The area is cleaned to bare metal and examined with magnetic particle testing, while ultrasonic testing or TOFD shows whether a crack runs into a thick butt weld below the surface. Crack length, frame location and the condition of earlier repairs are recorded so class can judge whether the repair approach should change.

sections.h: Thick deck plating and crack arrest on large container ships (UR S33)
p: As container ships grew, the upper flange needed steel more than 50 mm thick, and in thick plate a brittle crack starting in a heavy butt weld can run a long way before anything stops it. IACS responded with UR S33, Requirements for Use of Extremely Thick Steel Plates in Container Ships, for ships contracted for construction on or after 1 January 2014. It covers upper deck plating, the hatch side coaming and the coaming top in YP36, YP40 and YP47 steels over 50 mm and up to 100 mm thick; thicker plate falls under each society's own procedures.

Depending on steel and thickness, the measures include ultrasonic testing during construction of the block-to-block butt joints in the upper flange, to IACS Recommendation No. 20, and crack arrest design: arrest steel in the upper deck, coaming and deck block butts shifted at least 300 mm apart, crack arrest holes or arrest insert plates, with enhanced NDT such as TOFD as an alternative in some combinations. Periodic NDT after delivery can be required at the society's discretion.

For an owner, the point is to know which arrangement the ship was built with, because a repair that fills an arrest hole, lines up staggered butts or substitutes an ordinary grade can undo the design. Repairs in this region are planned with class and the yard against the original concept.

sections.h: Cell guides, lashing bridges and container securing points
p: Cell guides are the vertical angle bars that hold container stacks in the holds, with flared entry guides at the top. They take repeated knocks during cargo operations, and the common findings are bent or twisted angles, cracked brackets where guides attach to bulkheads or web frames, and torn entry guides. A bent guide jams boxes and leaves slots unused, so alignment is checked against the ship's tolerances as well as by eye.

Lashing bridges on the coamings or between bays suffer contact damage, corroded gratings and fatigue at their foot connections. Deck and tank-top sockets, D-rings and lashing eyes are welded attachments, examined for weld cracks and wastage of the plating around them. Loose lashing gear is the crew's responsibility under the ship's Cargo Securing Manual; an owner's inspection checks that the records match what is on board.

sections.h: Pontoon hatch covers: bearing pads, stoppers, cleats and seals
p: Most container ships use steel pontoon covers lifted off by the terminal's crane, many carrying several tiers of containers. That load passes into the coaming through bearing pads, and stoppers and, on many ships, cleats keep the covers in place. Worn or missing pads, cracked stopper brackets, distorted cover edges, corroded top plating and damaged container fittings are the recurring findings, and coaming drain channels block and corrode.

UR Z7 includes steel pontoons, cleats and their securing devices in the annual survey, and the third special survey adds thickness measurement of covers and coamings. On covers built with deliberate clearances between panels, seals are judged against the maker's drawing; fully gasketed covers can be tightness-tested ultrasonically. Gauging is far easier once a cover is landed on the quay, so the docking plan should say when covers come off.

sections.h: Ballast tanks, double bottoms and the spaces where defects appear
p: The double bottom is divided into ballast and fuel tanks, and the torsion box side tanks are usually ballast spaces. Frequent ballasting to manage trim, heel and draught on liner rotations keeps them wet, and once a hard coating is in POOR condition and not repaired, UR Z7 puts the tank on annual examination. Heated fuel tanks beside ballast spaces corrode faster on the shared boundary. The table brings together where defects usually appear on a container ship.

sections.h: Bow flare and the fore and aft ends of large container ships
p: Pronounced bow flare keeps the forward bays dry, but in heavy weather it slams into waves. The results are buckled shell panels between frames, cracked frame-to-stringer connections and damage to the breakwater and foremost stacks. Inside the forepeak and the spaces behind the flare, inspection records set-in plating and tripped stiffeners by frame so they can be followed at later surveys; forepeak internals join the UR Z7 minimum gauging from the third special survey.

At the aft end, the change from open cargo region to enclosed engine room structure is another stress concentration, with propeller-excited vibration adding cyclic load, so aft hatch corners deserve the same attention as those amidships.

sections.h: What owners check at charter redelivery and before a sale
p: At redelivery, owners and charterers compare the ship with the on-hire record: stevedore damage to cell guides, coamings, cover stoppers and lashing bridges, sockets, lashing gear against the inventory, and the reefer plant. Thermography of reefer switchboards and socket panels under load, and vibration readings on reefer and ventilation fans, add a condition record of those items.

A buyer looks further back: class status and conditions of class, hatch corner crack and repair history, earlier thickness reports, crack arrest records on larger ships and ballast tank coating condition. Together they say more about the next five years than the ship's age does.

Atlantis NDT supports these checks through pre-purchase inspections, vessel condition surveys and its Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme (CVIP), an owner-commissioned whole-ship condition assessment, sending teams from India to the ship for each job. No classification society has yet granted Atlantis UR Z17 approval; the company is in the process of obtaining it from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS, and until a certificate arrives its gauging informs the owner's planning without being credited to any class survey. faqs.q: Are container ships part of the enhanced survey programme?
faqs.a: No. The enhanced survey programme under SOLAS chapter XI-1 covers bulk carriers and oil tankers, and class extends it to chemical tankers. Dedicated container ships are surveyed under the general hull requirements of UR Z7. The extents are less prescriptive, so the owner's records of suspect areas, earlier cracks and coating breakdown have more influence on where the surveyor asks for close-up survey and readings.

faqs.q: Why do container ships crack at the hatch corners?
faqs.a: Because the hatch openings remove most of the deck, the plating left at each corner carries concentrated stress from hull bending and twisting. Any notch at the corner edge, such as a rough cut, a spatter mark or a corrosion pit, can start a fatigue crack that grows with each loading cycle. Such cracks usually show as broken paint before anything else, and are confirmed by magnetic particle testing on cleaned steel.

faqs.q: What is UR S33 and does it apply to my ship?
faqs.a: UR S33 sets requirements for extremely thick steel plates in container ships, covering upper deck and hatch coaming members over 50 mm and up to 100 mm thick in YP36, YP40 and YP47 steels. It applies to container ships contracted for construction on or after 1 January 2014. Whether a ship has arrest steel, staggered butts or arrest holes depends on its steel and plate thickness, and its construction records will show it.

faqs.q: Who inspects cell guides and lashing gear?
faqs.a: Cell guides are hull structure and are seen by class at surveys, but damage happens daily, so the crew and superintendents track it between surveys and arrange repairs. Loose lashing gear is the crew's responsibility under the Cargo Securing Manual. An owner's inspection at redelivery or before a sale checks both, recording bent guides, cracked attachments and gear shortfalls against the inventory.

faqs.q: How often are container ship hatch covers surveyed?
faqs.a: Hatch covers and coamings are examined at every annual survey under UR Z7, including steel pontoons, cleats and securing devices, with random operational checks. The special survey adds close-up survey of cover plating and coamings and a hose test or equivalent of the seals, and from the third special survey the minimum thickness measurement extent includes hatch covers and coamings.

faqs.q: What should a buyer ask for when inspecting a second-hand container ship?
faqs.a: The class status and survey records, earlier thickness measurement reports, the history of hatch corner and coaming cracks with their repair method, construction records for crack arrest features on larger ships, ballast tank coating condition and the reefer plant records. An inspection on board then confirms the condition of the structure those records describe, and looks at the areas they leave out.
